passages.happening:
When Samuel grows old, he makes his sons judges over Israel. Joel and Abijah judge at Beersheba. ‘But his sons did not walk in his ways; they turned aside toward dishonest gain, accepting bribes and perverting justice’ (verse 3).

All the elders of Israel come to Samuel at Ramah. “Look,” they said, “you are old, and your sons do not walk in your ways. Now appoint a king to judge us like all the other nations” (verse 5).

Samuel is displeased, and he prays (verse 6). The LORD answers: “Listen to the voice of the people in all that they say to you. For it is not you they have rejected, but they have rejected Me as their king” (verse 7). They have done the same ever since he brought them out of Egypt, forsaking him and serving other gods (verse 8).

‘Now listen to them, but you must solemnly warn them and show them the manner of the king who will reign over them’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
This chapter is the hinge of the whole book. Everything before it is the last chapter of the age of the judges. Everything after it concerns the kings.

The story repeats itself with a twist. Eli's sons were corrupt priests. Samuel's sons are corrupt judges. Taking bribes broke the law of Moses directly, which says a bribe ‘blinds the eyes of the wise’ (Deuteronomy 16:19). Beersheba, where they judged, was at the southern edge of Israel's land, far from their father at Ramah.

The request came late in the eleventh century BC, when Israel was pressed by the Philistines in the west and, as chapter 11 will show, the Ammonites in the east. The peoples around Israel had kings or strong rulers who could raise armies. A loose alliance of tribes, led by a judge from time to time, must have looked weak. The elders' reason is plainly military, and it will come out in full in verse 20.

In the ancient world a king was not only a ruler. He was seen as chosen by the gods, sometimes as a son of the gods, and as the link between the gods and the people. The law of Moses had looked ahead to this request and set limits on a king: he must be chosen by God, must not pile up horses, wives or wealth, and must read and keep the law. That law even imagines the people saying they want a king like all the nations around them, almost the elders' own words.

The elders were the leaders of the tribes and clans, with real authority. They are not rebels. They have a real problem, and they bring it to Samuel. The trouble is the answer they have already chosen.
passages.later:
The law of the king begins with the people's own words: “Let us set a king over us like all the nations around us” (Deuteronomy 17:14). It answers that they are to appoint ‘the king whom the LORD your God shall choose’ (Deuteronomy 17:15).

Gideon, offered a crown in the book of Judges, had refused it: “I will not rule over you, nor will my son. The LORD shall rule over you” (Judges 8:23).
passages.hard:
If the law of Moses allows Israel to have a king, why is asking for one treated as rejecting God?

The chapter seems to condemn what the law permits, and readers have explained the tension in several ways. One view looks at the motive and the timing. The problem is not kingship itself but a demand to be like the nations and a failure to trust God to save them, made while God was leading them through Samuel. The law required a king the LORD would choose, and the elders ask Samuel to appoint one on their terms. A second view notes that God had promised kings in Israel's future (Genesis 17:6; 35:11; 49:10), and finds the fault in grasping for a king before God's time and before his chosen king, David. A third, common among critical scholars, sees the book combining older accounts with different attitudes to the monarchy, some favorable and some hostile, and reads the chapter as an honest record of Israel's mixed experience of its kings.

Across these views, the text is clear on two things. The request came from a failure to trust God as king. And God took up the kingship anyway.
passages.asks: The elders had a real problem and brought it to Samuel with the answer already chosen. Ask where you have come to God asking him to approve a plan you had made without him. And ask what it would mean to trust God as king before you go looking for someone to fight your battles.

passages.happening:
Samuel tells the people everything the LORD said. “This will be the manner of the king who will reign over you: He will take your sons and appoint them to his own chariots and horses, to run in front of his chariots” (verse 11).

The list goes on. The king will make some officers and others farmers for his land and makers of his weapons (verse 12). ‘And he will take your daughters to be perfumers, cooks, and bakers’ (verse 13). He will take the best of their fields and vineyards and olive groves and give them to his servants (verse 14). He will take a tenth of their grain and their flocks, their servants and their best cattle, and ‘you yourselves will become his slaves’ (verses 15-17).

“When that day comes, you will beg for relief from the king you have chosen, but the LORD will not answer you on that day” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
The speech is built on one verb: take. It comes again and again, until it ends in the word slaves. Israel had been slaves in Egypt. Samuel warns that a king like the nations' kings would make them slaves again, in their own land.

The word for manner is the same word as justice in verse 3. Samuel's sons twisted justice, and the people want a king to give them justice. Samuel describes the king's justice, and it is taking.

The warning describes what kings in that world really did: calling up young men for the chariots and royal service, forced labor on royal land, a tax of a tenth of the harvest, and the seizing of property for royal officials. Scholars have compared it with royal records from the Canaanite city of Ugarit and elsewhere, and it fits the kingship known in Canaan in those centuries. Some scholars think the speech was shaped by Israel's later experience of Solomon's heavy demands. Others see it as a realistic warning drawn from the kingdoms Israel already knew.

These verses describe Israel's kingship under its covenant with God. They are not a program for any government or party today.
passages.later:
After Solomon's reign the northern tribes came to his son with the complaint Samuel had foreseen: “Your father put a heavy yoke on us. But now you should lighten the burden of your father’s service and the heavy yoke he put on us, and we will serve you” (1 Kings 12:4).

Centuries later Hosea looked back on Israel's kings and heard God say, ‘So in My anger I gave you a king, and in My wrath I took him away’ (Hosea 13:11).
passages.asks: Samuel warned that the king they wanted would take and keep taking. Ask what you have wanted badly enough to ignore what it would cost. And ask who, in your own small sphere, you take from when you could serve.

passages.happening:
The people refuse to listen to Samuel. “No!” they said. “We must have a king over us. Then we will be like all the other nations, with a king to judge us, to go out before us, and to fight our battles” (verses 19-20).

Samuel listens to all they say and repeats it to the LORD (verse 21). “Listen to their voice,” the LORD said to Samuel. “Appoint a king for them” (verse 22). And Samuel sends everyone home.
passages.hearers:
The verb to listen runs through the chapter. Three times the LORD tells Samuel to listen to the people's voice (verses 7, 9 and 22), and the people refuse to listen to Samuel (verse 19). Whether Israel and its king will listen to God becomes the test of the kingship from here on.

The people's last words show what they want: to be like everyone else, and to have someone else fight their battles. In the book of Judges, the LORD had fought Israel's battles. Now they want a king to do it.

God gives them what they ask. He grants a request he disapproves of, and he will work through it. Sometimes letting people have what they ask for is itself a judgment. Yet God does not abandon them. He will give a king, and later he will make the throne of David the carrier of his promise.
passages.later: Paul, preaching in Acts, tells it in one line: “Then the people asked for a king, and God gave them forty years under Saul son of Kish, from the tribe of Benjamin” (Acts 13:21).
passages.asks: God said to Samuel, ‘Listen to their voice.’ Ask whether God has ever let you have what you insisted on, and what you learned. And ask whose voice you listen to most when you decide what you need.
